entities.name: Johann Heinrich von Thünen
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Johann Heinrich von Thünen (1783–1850) was a Mecklenburg landowner-economist whose Isolated State model founded location theory and modern spatial economics. Observing his estate at Tellow, he formalised how transport costs and land rent organise concentric rings of agricultural land use around a central market—forestry, cropping, and grazing ordered by perishability and haulage.

Thünen combined careful farm accounts with abstract geometry, anticipating marginal analysis and the idea that location is an economic variable. Later urban and regional economists generalised his rings into industrial and residential location theory.

He remains the classic bridge between agrarian empiricism and mathematical economic geography.

entities.summary: Johann Heinrich von Thünen, a native of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, now in northern Germany, was a prominent nineteenth-century economist. Born on June 24, 1783, in Waddewarden, he studied agronomy and economics at the University of Göttingen. Von Thünen's magnum opus, 'Der Isolirte Staat' (The Isolated State), published in 1807, laid the foundation for modern economic thought on trade and spatial relationships. His influential work on the economic effects of geographical location and the distribution of labor, capital, and consumption influenced economists such as David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus. Von Thünen's contributions to economics have had a lasting impact on our understanding of global trade and the modern concept of the 'core-periphery' model. His work continues to be studied and applied in various fields, including geography, urban planning, and international trade. The concept of 'von Thünen's circle,' which describes the optimal spatial arrangement of economic activities, remains a fundamental principle in geography and economics. Von Thünen's legacy extends beyond academia, as his ideas have shaped modern economic policy and continue to inform global trade agreements. As a result, his work remains a crucial component of economic history and a testament to the power of intellectual curiosity and innovation.
